quests.ruleExplanation: Close opens the sentence with no stated subject (you is understood), followed directly by the object the door.
quests.nativeTip: Commands start directly with the base verb — no subject needed at all.

quests.ruleExplanation: Turn off is a phrasal verb that opens the command as one unit, followed by the object the lights.
quests.nativeTip: A phrasal verb like turn off stays together, right at the start of the command.

quests.ruleExplanation: Submit opens the command, your application is the object, and before Friday (a deadline) closes the sentence.
quests.nativeTip: The command can end with a deadline, even though it still starts with the base verb.

quests.ruleExplanation: Don't opens the negative command before touch, with the wet paint as the object.
quests.nativeTip: Don't opens a negative command, right before the base verb — no subject is used here either.

quests.ruleExplanation: Don't precedes forget, with your umbrella as the object, warning against forgetting something.
quests.nativeTip: The same don't-plus-base-verb pattern applies to any negative instruction.

quests.ruleExplanation: Don't precedes leave, with your bags unattended as the object, including a describing word after the noun.
quests.nativeTip: Don't still opens the command, even with a descriptive word at the end of the object.

quests.ruleExplanation: Please opens the sentence before arrive, softening the command into a polite request from the very first word.
quests.nativeTip: Please can open the sentence, softening the command right from the start.

quests.ruleExplanation: Please closes the sentence after a comma, following fasten your seatbelt — the same softening effect as opening with please, just at the other end.
quests.nativeTip: Please can also close the sentence, set off by a comma, for the same softening effect.

quests.ruleExplanation: Please opens the sentence before keep the noise down, a phrasal-verb command softened by please at the start.
quests.nativeTip: Please opens the sentence here too, right before the phrasal verb.

quests.ruleExplanation: First fronts the instruction, followed by a comma and the command turn on the machine, showing this is the opening step.
quests.nativeTip: A sequencing word like first can front an instruction, set off by a comma, before the command itself.

quests.ruleExplanation: Then fronts the instruction, followed by a comma and add the ingredients slowly, marking the next step after the first.
quests.nativeTip: Then works the same way, marking this as the next step in a sequence.

quests.ruleExplanation: Finally fronts the instruction, followed by a comma and press the start button, marking the last step in the sequence.
quests.nativeTip: Finally signals the last step, still fronting the sentence before the comma and command.

quests.ruleExplanation: Could opens the request before you, with close the window following in normal verb-object order.
quests.nativeTip: Could inverts to the front, before you, to soften a command into a polite request.

quests.sentence: Could you send me the invoice?
quests.ruleExplanation: Could opens the request before you, and send me the invoice follows, with me and the invoice as indirect and direct objects.
quests.nativeTip: The same pattern works with a double object after the base verb.

quests.ruleExplanation: Could opens the request before you, repeat that follows, and please closes the sentence after a comma for extra politeness.
quests.nativeTip: Please can still close the sentence after a comma, even within a could-you request.

quests.ruleExplanation: Would you mind requires the -ing form waiting (not the base verb wait), making this an especially polite request.
quests.nativeTip: Would you mind is followed by the -ing form of the verb, not the base form.

quests.sentence: Would you mind lowering your voice?
quests.ruleExplanation: Would you mind precedes lowering (the -ing form), with your voice as the object.
quests.nativeTip: The same -ing rule applies here: mind is always followed by a gerund.

quests.sentence: Would you mind checking the schedule?
quests.ruleExplanation: Would you mind precedes checking (the -ing form), with the schedule as the object.
quests.nativeTip: Mind still takes the -ing form, regardless of which verb or object follows.

quests.ruleExplanation: Let's opens the suggestion, including the speaker in the action, followed by review the numbers together.
quests.nativeTip: Let's proposes an action that includes the speaker, followed directly by the base verb.

quests.ruleExplanation: Let's precedes take, with a short break as the object, suggesting a shared action.
quests.nativeTip: The same let's-plus-base-verb pattern makes a shared suggestion.

quests.sentence: Let's schedule the meeting for Monday.
quests.ruleExplanation: Let's precedes schedule, with the meeting as the object and for Monday closing the sentence.
quests.nativeTip: Let's still opens the suggestion, even with a time expression at the end.

quests.sentence: Make sure to lock the door.
quests.ruleExplanation: Make sure to precedes lock (base form), with the door as the object, emphasizing the importance of the action.
quests.nativeTip: Make sure to is followed by the base form of the verb, giving a firm instruction.

quests.sentence: Make sure to save your work.
quests.ruleExplanation: Make sure to precedes save (base form), with your work as the object.
quests.nativeTip: The same pattern applies to any important instruction using make sure to.

quests.sentence: Make sure to arrive early tomorrow.
quests.ruleExplanation: Make sure to precedes arrive (base form), with early tomorrow closing the sentence.
quests.nativeTip: Make sure to still leads into the base verb, even with a time word at the end.

quests.sentence: Report to the front desk by nine.
quests.ruleExplanation: Report opens the instruction, to the front desk (place) follows, and by nine (time) closes it, extending the imperative into a full place-time chain.
quests.nativeTip: The command opens with the verb, then where to go, then by what time.

quests.sentence: Leave your luggage at the counter.
quests.ruleExplanation: Leave opens the instruction, your luggage is the object, and at the counter (place) closes the sentence.
quests.nativeTip: The object comes right after the verb, then the place where it should go.

quests.sentence: Submit the form at our office before noon.
quests.ruleExplanation: Submit opens the instruction, the form is the object, at our office (place) follows, and before noon (time) closes it.
quests.nativeTip: Stack object, then place, then time, just as in earlier statement-based sentences from this curriculum.

quests.sentence: First, make sure to check your passport.
quests.ruleExplanation: First fronts the instruction with a comma, followed by make sure to check your passport, combining two skills from this file.
quests.nativeTip: Combine a fronted sequencing word with a make-sure-to instruction.

quests.sentence: Could you please turn down the volume?
quests.ruleExplanation: Please sits between you and turn down here, showing a third possible position for please beyond the sentence-opening and sentence-closing spots seen earlier.
quests.nativeTip: Please can also sit in the middle of a request, right between you and the verb.

quests.sentence: Don't forget to submit the form before Friday.
quests.ruleExplanation: Don't forget opens the negative command, to submit the form (an infinitive phrase) follows, and before Friday (deadline) closes the sentence.
quests.nativeTip: Combine a negative command with an infinitive and a deadline at the end.
